review:
Two words... Dark and Creepy. Little Nightmares is far from a horror game, but does just enough to make you feel uncomfortable while you're playing it. Set in a morbid cruise ship from hell where the guests like to feast on the flesh of children while they pig out like animals, you'll find yourself escaping from humanoid like creatures that truly are the products of nightmares. The story is amazing and you'll be left shocked and dumbfounded at the end, not really knowing what's going on because very little is actually explained, but enjoying every second of it nonetheless. The DLC's add even more onto that sentiment, leaving you in a state of despair and questioning yourself, why are we even here... just to suffer?

Suffering and creepy elements aside, Little Nightmares truly is a beautifully done game with detailed artwork that breathes life into the dead carcass that is the Maw... you'll definitely want to play this one with the lights off though. The soundtrack only adds onto that, raising your heartbeat the closer you get to danger was something that really made me feel all the more immersed into the story and the ambient noises make sure you're always feeling tense as you traverse the the darkness. 

The gameplay itself however felt like the only shortcoming this game had, at least in my opinion. More than the unearthly local residents of the Maw, the number one thing that always got me killed was falling due to bad camera angles and choppy controls that would lead me plummeting to a premature demise. Being an Indie 3Dish puzzle-solving platformer I know I shouldn't be too demanding, but there was just something about the puzzles that didn't resonate with me... most of the time just by glancing around the room you would know exactly what to do and you could just breeze through all the chapters like there was no tomorrow, the whole game could probably be completed in about 2 hours (+1 hour w/ DLC's) so you'll definitely end up with a feeling of wanting more.

That being said, Little Nightmares is still one hell of a game and I would most definitely recommend it to anyone who's thinking of giving it a try, but because of the moderate price and short length of the game I would suggest waiting for it to go on discount and buying the Complete Edition to get the most value out of your money.

[h1]Little Nightmares[/h1]

Our main character, Six, in a yellow raincoat, tries to escape from a ship named Maw, fictionalized with the horrors of our childhood nightmares. Although Little Nightmares resembles Playdead's Limbo and Inside at first glance, with a side-scrolling head adorned with little boy and platform elements, it is thematically different from its cousins..

The carefully designed parts of Little Nightmares, whose tension never decreases, contain different nightmares. Who is not on this ship? For example; A ship janitor with short legs but arms several meters long? Of course. Or a cook who looks grotesque and is always at the meat-cutting or eating ceremony? There is room. An older sister wearing a kimono like from Japanese horror movies? Don't be! The design of every scene we meet with these friends is designed in the quality of a painting where Bob Ross expresses his art: careful and ingenious.

Little Nightmares does not contain any fighting mechanics as we are used to this type of game. When you move from scenes that are designed like a toy house to another, you need to analyze the surroundings well and think about how to get out of the nightmare this time. You always do the indispensable actions of platform games, such as finding movement levers and running platforms, climbing the steps with the help of a box. Of course, your enemies do not collect pears while you are doing these in the nauseating rooms of the Maw ship, such as the room of the cook and his wife, inside the pipes, the garbage dump where the shoes are collected (though the janitor does not collect pear balls with those arms). Taking advantage of the small size of the Six, you should always hide in the shadows and the smallest holes and not appear to the enemies. It's okay to be a fodder to these staff at the slightest mistake.

[b]Are we the Little Nightmare?[/b]

I did not have any difficulties in terms of privacy throughout the game. Once you learn the enemies' routines, it is easy to get past them by staying in the shadows, but the most important thing that makes Little Nightmares unique is the use of the fear factor. Most games and movies try to achieve fear by not showing us what we fear. When we are looking for the key to the locked door with a lantern in a dark corridor, what frightens us is to think about when the enemy will come, shouting at the house boards with his steps. Little Nightmares, on the other hand, always puts the enemy in front of you, turning the factor of fear from when to every moment. In some scenes the main event is outside the camera's angle and you have to move the camera to the edge of the scene using the right-stick to see it. So in a way you are going to the fear you expect. Also, the scripted scenes in the game host perhaps the most terrifying moments I've seen in a side-scrolling / horror game. In these scenes reminiscent of a cat-and-mouse chase, the play's magnificent soundtrack does not do its best to rivet the atmosphere.

I know I haven't talked too much into the story of the game. I do this specifically because Little Nightmares is not a very long game anyway. I was able to see the end of the game over a period of three hours in one sitting. The story goes to very interesting places towards the end. Although my mouth was not open when the story of the game was over, a devilish smile appeared on my face. I'm talking vaguely because I don't want to be too explicit, but if you're playing indie games for their stories, Little Nightmare won't disappoint you.

So I praised the game but why is the score 8? Because although Little Nightmares does very well what it does well, it doesn't have some annoying flaws. Perhaps the most annoying part of the game is the automatic recording system, which sometimes takes very long periods in between. I said I finished the game in 3 hours, I suppose half an hour of that was spent by dying at the end of the episode, falling into the saint of the bad recording system and doing everything over again. Also, since the game takes the recordings before the 15-20 seconds of preparation at the beginning of the stage entries, you have to repeat these non-passed parts in every unsuccessful attempt. Besides that, the platform gameplay isn't that great either. While I didn't have too much trouble, Six sometimes resisted not keeping the item I wanted. Also, pressing two keys simultaneously to climb started to tire my hand holding the gamepad after a while.

Little Nightmares has managed to gather both side-scrolls, horror and mysterious story lovers in the same ship. When the creepy atmosphere riveted with its magnificent visuals and music, a game that would be a candidate for being a classic came out.

[i]Pros[/i]

• The perfect and chilling atmosphere.
• An intriguing and immersive story.
• Oh those visuals! Amazing art design, too.

[i]Cons[/i]

• Some puzzles can cause confusion due to perspective issues.
• Seems a little short? When the game was over, I felt like I was not done with the game.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]

• Little Nightmares is not a game that will shake your world, but it definitely brings a new breath to both side-scrolling platformers and horror games genre.

The game was originally called "Hunger", then developers realized it would be a bit hard to find the game on Google search. Little Nightmare is more suitable for the title because of how small the children are compare to creepy monster in this game

It's more creepy than scary. Some things might spook and surprise you, but overall it's not that scary. It's an atmospheric game where you have to kind of map out everything in your brain and just try different paths until you are correct, but be ready to flee!

I may just be a big softie, but this little protagonist girl, Six, is represented as the unlikely hero. I spend most of the game wanting to protect her from getting caught by creepy monsters. There are also innocent children, called Nomes, hiding in dark places. They have no purpose beyond trying to survive.

There is almost no music during the gameplay which brings a lot of elements to your ears. Personally, I love this! If you're not careful, you will hear ambient anxiety inside your head. What is more impressive is that the entire spooky tale is played out without the use of any dialogue or text. Everything is relegated to visual pleasure experience.

Little Nightmare sets only one goal: escape. Delivering a great story and stunning ambiance, this title impresses until the very end and, to date,  is probably the best of its genre. Sadly, the game mechanics aren't par with the art direction, and nothing will really motivate players to invest more time than needed for its short initial play through. As a narrative experience, though, it won't disappoint and leave you begging for more. 

Recommended on sales, or for any fan of ambient platformers (Limbo, Inside, Spate...)

You literally start at Six. Six, a little yellow running hooded girl spawning from a suitcase, and fated to escape The Maw, a facility which goal is best left uncovered for now. The first impression the game gives is awe for its fantastic polish and esthetic, reminding the player of a Tim Burton stop motion movie. Six has to hide, run and solve a number of puzzles in order to get out, and does so thanks to her strong little legs and arms, equipped with nothing else than a lighter (which, really is only there to add to the ambiance). 

Here, no jumping on enemy heads to flatten them, no bullets, and generally more escape than confrontation. Little Nightmares is all about finding the right timing, remaining silent, and not getting noticed by the grotesque and deformed hosts of The Maw. Although wordless, Little Nightmares was developped as an interactive story, apparently based around the feelings of inadequacy one can feel when transing from childhood to early adulthood. Everything is exaggerated, disproportionate, and, of course, nightmarish.

As with all games of its kind (Limbo, Intside, Spate, etc...) the ambiance is the major selling point of this title, and it actually manages to take its proposition to the next level: everything, from sounds to physics, is here to make players feel ill at ease and, as a result, the fear of the unknown might very well crawl inside their brains, especially when starting a new area. The visuals are absolutely in tune as well, as the Unreal Engine 4 is put to excellent use. Delivery wise, I would definitely consider this game as the best of its kind. 

Are fear and ambiance enough to make this game an absolute masterpiece though? I do not think so. To begin with, the major problem with its gameplay comes from the same daring camera angles that make its visuals so engrossing: Six will rather often err in an unwanted direction, or fall to her death, beacause of skewed perspective to which the controls aren't always adapted. 

Past this technical observation, I personally feel that this game bears a lot of unexploited potential. Why, for instance, give Six a lighter which she will never use to advance the plot? Why give an action button which will trigger everything in the game save one specific switch? And what about throwing items only used in a couple of cases? These under exploited mechanics, combined with the slow pace of the hide-and-seek phases, made me feel more relieved to be able to move to the next challenge rather than feel content as the result of having solved a well thought puzzle. 

All in all, I feel that the only real challenge of the game is the intermittent struggle against the camera's perspective, and that, with these fantastic physics and ambiance, play time could have been considerably lenghtened by the use more-than-just-simplistic puzzles. As it is, the game is as good as its story, and there is no motivation to return to it once the final chapter has been closed. 

Even with its low replayability level and strong 'ambiance over action' concept, it remains that Little Nightmares successfully reaches its goals by delivering an interesting methaphorical story, great immersion and overal gameplay which will most likely trigger real emotions (mostly disgust, but the fun kind).

I would recomend it to ambient platformer fans as a must play game, and for all others I would definitely suggest to grab it on sales as it is a definite milestone in the genre.

[h1]Story[/h1]
In Little Nightmares, you take control of Six, a young girl who awakens in a panic after a startling dream about a tall, thin woman standing in thick shadow, who slowly turns to realise her.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3143300160

With Six dragging herself from her bed, you are tasked with helping her escape The Maw that has become her home. Complete puzzles while being pursued by the many residents who wish to seek Six harm, evade your pursuers and help her attain the freedom she desires.

Little Nightmares is a wonderfully designed story experience that is captivatingly innocent and ruthlessly dark, all in a seamless brushstroke. By capturing a tangible yearning to escape the confines forced upon you, this game illustrates a true struggle to survive in its absolute primal form, employing your childhood fears and uncomfortable settings to throw you off and forcing you to question whether the next step will be your last.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[h3]A game of cat and mouse.[/h3]
Six has very little in her favour aboard The Maw. She is small, unarmed and weak to the many horrors that seek her demise. Even in the aspects you would believe would be on her side, such as speed and agility, she still falls short compared to them. The only real option you have to keep her safe is to keep her hidden by hiding in the shadows and embracing claustrophobic tunnels.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3143300269

A task often made difficult by the fact the movement controls are a touch cumbersome and often make it challenging to manoeuvre as you seek your escape.

Thankfully, exploration doesn't play a large part in the experience here, so you won't have to go far off the beaten track often to find items or collectibles.

[h3]Use your head.[/h3]
The only other significant aspect of this game is the puzzle mechanics. There are quite a few puzzles in Little Nightmares that will challenge you to complete multiple steps for your reward or have you try and achieve objectives while being hunted.

These can be quite difficult to overcome, but the reward for your prowess and ingenuity will be your freedom.

[h1]Audio and Visual[/h1]
As mentioned above, Little Nightmares does suffer from somewhat dated graphics, but it is far from a terrible visual experience. The journey is still extremely captivating and atmospheric, and it plays like it’s right at home on the deck.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3143300584

The audio hasn't aged as much and remains a solid experience throughout the journey. Animation sounds will have you gritting your teeth against the abrasive sounds you commit to, and the general ambience of the world helps immerse you wholly. The music is also sensational by providing compelling and unique tracks for each new location you visit.

[h1]Deck Performance and Specifications[/h1]
I experienced no issues running Little Nightmares on the deck, and the general performance was well above expectations. A full charge allowed approximately 3-4 hours of gameplay at the default graphical settings.

[h1]It feels a bit like Ghibli with the creepiness factor dialled way up [/h1]

Little Nightmares is an atmospheric adventure game from Tarsier Studios. It’s been out since 2017 and I picked it up last year with the intention of playing through it with my girlfriend, but we never got very far with it. Seeing it on the store page this weekend got me interested in it again, so I decided to pick it back up. I’ve completed the main game and I’ve now picked up all the DLC, it’s a great little game.

[h1]Positives: [/h1]
[list][*]The art is just fantastic, this is creepy eye candy all the way. They did a really good with textures and everything, but the game is really made by the lighting, it’s well used to create a very creepy atmosphere. 

[*]Speaking of atmosphere, the music and sound in the game is also really well done to help create that creepiness throughout the game. The ‘voice acting’ is really great here, it’s easy to make monsters sound cheesy but it was really well done here.

[*]The monsters are where I draw my comparison to Ghibli from. They really remind me of some of the villains from the Ghibli movies, and I’m pretty sure that one of the latter sections of the game is at least partially inspired by Spirited Away. But yeah, the monsters are really well designed, and I definitely found them very creepy.

 [*]I’m glad that they stuck with atmospheric horror rather than going for scares, it works much better for this style of game I reckon. I’m a bit of a wimp when it comes to horror games, so I really enjoyed being able to explore this horrific world without the threat of things jumping out at me. I mean, there are things that jump out at you, but this isn’t a jump-scare kind of game.

[*]It’s short. I can kind of understand why people would be a bit put off by a $15 game that’s only about three hours long, but I really don’t think this game would benefit from being longer. This is another one that delivers a great experience in a shorter period of time, and it never feels like a slog or that it overstays its welcome. Plus, on sale you can get the base game and the DLC for $9 now, which is great value.

[*]The controls are good, which is obviously important for a 2.5D game. There were a couple of points, particularly when walking on thing walkway type things, that it was a bit tricky. But overall, I didn’t have much trouble with it.

[*]Unless I missed something, it’s pretty light on story, but I don’t think that’s a bad thing. The journey the game takes you on is more than enough, and I thought the ending was excellent. [/list]

[h1]Negatives: [/h1]
[list][*]I did have a couple of issues with fullscreen, sometimes when I would click on the screen it would pull me back to windows as I had somehow clicked something on the desktop/taskbar. It didn’t happen too often, but it was frustrating when it did.

[*]There are a few segments in the game where you have to run from or to something. Most of these segments are good, and create tension, but there were a couple that I found frustrating. I don’t want to spoil the game though, so I won’t say anymore. [/list]

[h1]Verdict: [/h1]

All in all, Little Nightmares is an excellent little game. It takes you on an incredibly creepy journey through a very unpleasant ship, and it looks damn good doing it. I’d recommend it at full price, but this is definitely a must buy when it’s on sale.

[b]Little Nightmares[/b] is an enthralling and atmospheric puzzle-platformer that will leave players spellbound with its hauntingly unique visuals and eerie ambience. The attention to detail in the game's design is commendable, immersing players in a foreboding atmosphere that feels like a living nightmare. The use of lighting and shadows adds to the overall haunting experience, making every moment visually stunning and memorable.

The game's storyline is shrouded in mystery, which works to its advantage. Players control Six, a small, vulnerable protagonist who must navigate through the twisted halls of The Maw – a vast, derelict vessel inhabited by sinister and grotesque creatures. The lack of exposition allows players to unravel the narrative at their own pace, keeping them engaged and eager to discover the secrets hidden within the game's world.

Gameplay-wise, [b]Little Nightmares[/b] excels in creating a tense and suspenseful experience. Players must rely on their wits and stealth to avoid danger and solve environmental puzzles. The game strikes a perfect balance between challenging puzzles and nerve-wracking encounters, keeping players on their toes throughout the adventure.

The sound design deserves special mention for enhancing the game's chilling atmosphere. The haunting melodies and spine-chilling sound effects further immerse players in the twisted world of [b]Little Nightmares[/b], creating an emotional connection with the game that lasts long after the credits roll.

However, [b]Little Nightmares[/b] isn't without its flaws. Some players might find the controls a bit clunky at times, leading to frustrating moments during high-stress situations. Additionally, the game's brevity might leave players wanting more, as the journey can be completed in just a few hours.

In conclusion, [b]Little Nightmares[/b] is a captivating experience that excels in creating an unforgettable and chilling adventure. With its striking art style, atmospheric world, and clever gameplay mechanics, it manages to immerse players in a hauntingly beautiful nightmare. Here's a quick, little platform-puzzle game somewhat in the same vein as "Limbo" and "Inside".

As a whole, I really liked this game... much like I enjoyed playing Limbo and Inside. Simple, platform-driven puzzles. Challenges that are compartmentalized from room to room. If I had to rank this game against the other two ("Limbo" and "Inside"), I think it just ekes out the competition. In fairness, they probably stand neck-and-neck in terms of challenge and overall fun, but what I really appreciated about "Little Nightmares" was the environment and character design. Shit's just so creepy, yet so beautiful. Probably helps the game is running on Unreal 4 game engine, but god-damn is it gorgeous. 

While this is not going to be my top game of 2017, it will rank high. And I would certainly recommend playing it if you're into puzzle platformers. Now, whether it's worth $20... that's debatable.

After finishing the short but sweet story of both Little Nightmares and its companion DLC "Secrets of the Maw", I was extremely surprised and sad that I hadn't heard or seen this game before. What had initially put this game on my radar was seeing it suggested in my discovery queue. It sat in my wishlist for the longest time, and only recently for the Halloween sale I bought it. I saw that it was on a super deep discount and knew that I would be losing money not buying it.

Initially booting up the game, I realized I knew nothing about it. I hadn't watched any reviews, gameplay walk-through, I don't even think I even read the steam description of the game. I was purely hooked on the screenshots from the steam page. That's saying something. I was solely hooked on the aesthetics of the game, and boy was I glad that was able to solely convince me on purchasing the game. What I didn't expect was the touching story, a wide variety of puzzles, and the spine-chilling hums the music tracks had to offer.

Typical for this genre of games, there is a story and deeper meaning that you can pick up while doing the various activities in-game. Pictures on the wall of horrid human-looking faces, frozen fear-struck children under a watchful eye, or the different disturbing enemies encountered throughout the different rooms, there is always something to look and ponder at. Along with these, there are the unforgettable gnomes running around the different areas, showing you how to solve a puzzle or even being a nice companion to just hug. These gnomes serve as the main focal point and are more expanded upon in the "Secrets of the Maw" DLC. Both stories of Little Nightmares and Secrets of the Maw provide an interesting and heart-string pulling narrative that the player is sure to take heart to. Each player might get different mileage out of the different campaigns, but I thought both were of high quality. If I had to choose which one I liked the most, I would have to choose Secrets of the Maw as my favorite in terms of story. I really enjoy stories that are set within the same time period of other ones, and seeing said stories of Six and Runaway Kid intertwine and mix in creative ways really emphasizes that the player needs to experience both of them to have the full Little Nightmares experience.
 
Now delving into the main meat and potatoes, or meat and gnome, of the game, the different puzzles. Both base game and DLC offer complex and elaborate puzzles in different forms. Some examples of the puzzles you'll encounter: filling up a furnace with the most amount of coal, how to turn off the power to get past the electric fence that it's powering, and trying to survive and sneak past the multiple monsters you will encounter. And this is where a lot of Little Nightmares gets its heart racing sweat dribbling down your face moments. When you walking into a dark room only lit by your tiny flashlight, and you come across a monster with long arms and a blindfold standing right in front of you, Nightmares uses its great atmosphere to send the player into a panic for what to do next and find a way out. Most of the time, the player is dumped right into the room with the enemy, and is tasked with trying to get out of the room by either not being seen by them or out running them. Overall, I really enjoyed most of the puzzles. Looking in retrospect, both games structure their puzzles differently, with Nightmares having more linear point A point B objectives, and Secrets being more open with multiple puzzles in one large area. I liked both styles of puzzles, but I really enjoyed what base game Nightmares had to offer more. That's not to say what Secrets had to offer was bad, I still enjoyed them and found them challenging, but I enjoyed the more linear style of the base game.

When I was initially hooked on the game's atmosphere, I was putting a lot of trust into the game. I wasn't considering the gameplay, the music, the story, I was trusting purely on the looks and how pretty it was. I wish that I had cared or thought to look at the other aspects that make this game so compelling.  The lighting, the music, the art style, and the sound are all what I would expect to see from a triple-A studio. Lighting was used to great effect, with the developers giving a small light source being a lighter or flashlight to most of the time light giant dark rooms. The way light sources bounce off of walls and are absorbed by the different objects gives the game a very realistic feeling, feeding into the glamor or cruddyness of each environment. Adding onto this with the soundtrack of the game, it sets the tone effortlessly. Just listing to the music alone brings me back to those moments from the game of walking through dark hallways and running from the different monsters. The edition that I bought sadly didn't include the soundtrack, but I totally see myself purchasing it when it goes on sale again. Finally looking at the art style, I really don't know what to say. Even with competing games out there sporting ultra-realistic graphics, Nightmares carries its own weight with it's cute but effective art style. If you like the styles of Tim Burton or movies like Caroline, you are sure to be a fan of this one and what it has to offer. 

While I've been looking at the positives for most of the review, there were a few negative parts to my experience. For starters, I had a few issues trying to traverse the world with the controls for the game. I played on a standard keyboard and mouse and didn't really have a problem until it came to moving the flashlight around in certain parts of the DLC. Climbing up and down certain ladders also proved to be a little nightmare for me. The rest of the controls of the game were fine, but these are just small things that could be worked on in a sequel. Another huge impact on my experience were the crashes. Sometimes my game would crash on the pause screen, and the only way to close the game was to do a full restart of my computer. This only happened about three times, but it really negatively impacted my experience, causing me to stop playing the game altogether for the night and continue later on. A few other nitpicks I had were things like the mouse going over from the game to my other screen causing me to have to pause the game fully and then go back to play, and the occasional bug. Most of these weren't detrimental to my experience, but I thought it was important to point out.

But to sum it up and put a nice little bow on top, I don't need to restate that I enjoyed this game again. It was a short but very pleasant and fun experience that I suggest any gamer or at least one someone that enjoys an experience enriched with creativity to indulge in anytime. While I do think that the game is fantastic and high quality, without being on sale I think that the price is really steep. As others have pointed out and as I have experienced, waiting for the game to go on sale is a great time to leap and buy the game. I wouldn't mind paying full price for the package, but I guess I did what a lot of others would do and just wait for the game to go on sale. It all depends on each person. The future for Little Nightmares going forward looks bright. Tarsier Studios have showcased and revealed a release date for Little Nightmares 2, and I am excited to see how the team can expand on their initial ideas. Most of all, I'm really interested to see how Tarsier incorporates newer technologies like ray tracing and faster load times to create an even better package than they've made before. The future looks bright, and I'd be lying if I said I wasn't a little excited.  

I hope this review helped you determine whether or not to purchase the game, and if you have any feedback or comments please feel free to leave them in the comments or contact me through steam. Thanks for reading!

Roll over, Playdead!

   Well...maybe not quite. But this is certainly the closest thing I've seen to the makers of Limbo and Inside having a legit competitor in the spooky side-scrolling puzzle-platformer stakes. Sure there's some other efforts which got a fair part of the way there - the underrated Feist and Buddy both spring immediately to mind - but this is the first game where I can safely say, "You like Playdead? I can almost GUARANTEE you will love this one to bits too." To say that Tarsier Studios has learned a trick or two from the other company is an understatement, but it's by no means a case of simple plagiarism.

   For starters, this game does something no Playdead game has done before: it's full-blown 3D, as opposed to the equally lovely-looking 2.5D. As well as moving left and right, our protagonist can move up and down, albiet in fairly limited three-dimensional spaces (so all you every-game-must-be-open-world whiners can just kindly fuck off, as with almost every other game I like). It's also a bit more of a stealth-horror game than either Playdead effort, with many sequences in which you're trying to solve a puzzle or find an item while being perpetually badgered by something ten times your size which can crush you in a single mighty fist. The game furthermore has its own distinct look and atmosphere: no young boys lacking in facial features for example (just a little girl with her face barely visible), and hey, it's not like Playdead have set an entire game on a boat before (okay, so I'm clutching at straws by this point, but full marks to me for trying).

   On the whole it's a tad more whimsical and cartoon-ish than Playdead's releases, but we still have that delightfully ruthless approach to killing our tiny protagonist at any and every opportunity. It's not quite as dark and brutal as Inside, though, so for those who felt that one pushed the boundaries of acceptable child abuse in a video gaming context, this might be a more suitable game to give to your young'uns to enjoy. It's also a tiny bit EASIER than the Playdead games, so again, may be a better place to start for those new to the perils of puzzle-platforming.

   A simply stunning debut from Tarsier, and one of the most cinematic and immersive games you will play this or any other year in the near future. Though fuck me, it is astonishing where games are heading, and if that VR nonsense ever gets embraced by the mainstream I think we can just forget about fully-functioning societies and resign ourselves to a world full of catheterized coma-cases laying on soiled sheets, with the lower slave classes rolling us over occasionally so we don't get bed sores. I, for one, cannot wait.

A cool game with great graphics and an interesting story.
It reminded me a lot of the game INSIDE in graphics and gameplay, and the animated film Spirited Away in story and theme.

As a puzzle/platformer I liked INSIDE a bit better. It had more clever and varied puzzles and mechanics. But this game is more detailed, immersive and less abstract, as in every object is modeled to look real and not just generic boxes and platforms like you get in most platformers. Every level has it's own distinct style. The perspective of the tiny weak girl looking up at the big, gruesome, deadly world around her keeps you on edge all the time. The levels look so disgusting and horrible you can almost smell it, but are beautiful at the same time. 
I really enjoyed sneaking through the dirty kitchen and outsmart the evil cook preparing his disgusting food. The atmosphere is perfect, it almost becomes tangible. The game is also at times very intense and exciting when you try to sneak past an enemy and run for cover when spotted.
The levels are well layed out, although linear. It's designed to be a straightforward rollercoaster of impressions and it works very well. Except when you die you sometimes respawn quite a way back which suddenly breaks the pace and is a bit frustrating, especially when you keep dying somewhere because the controls aren't working with you (see point below).

Gameplay-wise there could have been more variation. You will mostly be sneaking past enemies to get a key to open a door, or running away from them until you reach a tiny gap only you can fit through. I feel they could have made more intersting puzzels with those great environments and the Unreal physics engine. If it wasn't for the visuals every level would feel pretty much the same, apart from some moments. But the developers chose the immersive route over gameplay and I'm glad they did. The balance works well in the end.
This game was a pleasant surprise, and I would certainly recommend it.

Some negative points:
- Dying can set you back quite a bit sometimes, which can become a bit annoying if you keep dying. The savepoints could have been placed better.
- Where movement in INSIDE was strictly kept 2D, Little Nightmares let you also move towards and away from the camera, which opens up some more gameplay options and makes the game more immersive, but it also makes it more difficult see at where in space your character is in order to make a certain jump or hit a button. I was caught by an enemy or fell off a platform a lot of times because the character didn't go where I expected her to go. This struggle with the movement made the game in turn less immersive for me so I wish they kept it 2D.
- I didn't find a way to change key bindings, and as I play on keyboard I was stuck wit the arrow keys.
- I could play INSIDE on a keyboard but for the reasons above I would really recommend a controller for this one.
- The ending could have been better and the story could have used some explanation, but you could argue the uncertainty makes it more powerful.

But in the field of puzzles, we see the same creativity that we saw in a game like Inside, in Little Nightmares. It is true that the number of puzzles in the game is not very much, but the existing ones have an interesting design and are fun to solve.

During the game, we see antagonists who just need to see you to be killed. Their presence in the scene is enough to give you a sense of fear and try to take refuge in a safe corner immediately. As a result, in the game, you must first try not to be seen, and then, if you are seen, you must try to escape from the enemy in chases.

But in my opinion, the main part of Little Nightmares game is its story. After finishing the game, gamers will be divided into two groups. In terms of audio, the game is at a very good level, and the voiceovers are well and accurately performed and play a significant role in inducing a sense of fear in the game.

I initially wrote this game off as being another one of the short kid-focused horror games that were popular at the time, in the same vein as games like Five Nights at Freddy’s and Hello Neighbour.

Oh, how wrong I was.

[h1]A One of a Kind Nightmare[/h1]

Little Nightmares is, without a doubt, one of the most atmospheric and hauntingly beautiful games that I’ve ever played. The eerie world, oppressive, bleak, and surreal atmosphere, the unsettling characters, and the deeply immersive narrative all come together to create a truly unforgettable experience.

The game’s art style is striking, with its twisted, dreamlike, and timeless environments that are both captivating and terrifying. Each area is meticulously crafted to evoke a sense of dread, and the subtle details in the world-building make it feel alive, albeit in a nightmarish way. The use of lighting and sound adds layers to the atmosphere, with every creak, shadow, and distant noise keeping you on edge throughout the journey.

The art artstyle of both this game and its sequel reminded me heavily of the works of Lemony Snicket (Daniel Handler), specifically A Series of Unfortunate Events. Both the world described in the books and the art direction from the 2004 movie adaptation present a similar timeless and surreal aesthetic to Little Nightmares; both works even make heavy use of eye imagery, which is probably what made the connection for me.

In terms of character design, each of them fits the dreamlike twisted world perfectly. While I personally don’t really find any of the adults scary, maybe with the exception of the janitor, all of them are still very unsettling. Six is immediately an iconic design; while she still bears a resemblance to other characters, namely Coraline, she still manages to stand out from other horror protagonists with her yellow raincoat, dark hair that covers her eyes, shadowy face and Zippo lighter.

While the monstrous adults found in this game are not really terrifying to me, the real horror of this game, to me, is found in the unknown. What is this world, and how did it come to be? Throughout the game, you are given tidbits of lore which draw you in and make you think. Fear of the Unknown, coupled with the bleak, hopeless atmosphere, is what makes this game scary to me.

Little Nightmares boasts a marvellous soundtrack, where every track is meticulously tailored to its setting. Six's Theme, a recurring melody that can be found throughout the series, is especially impactful. Its progression, starting softly and building to a darker crescendo, powerfully reflects Six's emotional arc, illustrating her slow transformation from vulnerable child to one of the monsters she was trying so hard to escape from.

The gameplay itself is brilliant. It’s a mix of platforming, puzzle-solving, and stealth, all wrapped in a tense, claustrophobic atmosphere. The puzzles are not very challenging; I was never stuck for more than 10 minutes, but despite this, they still managed to be entertaining and illustrated the use of some grey greymatter. The stealth, on the other hand, is executed perfectly; sneaking past enemies in this game, especially the janitor, is a genuinely exhilarating experience. 

While the story is told in a subtle, almost cryptic way, it’s clear that Little Nightmares is about more than just escaping a nightmare. It’s a commentary on fear, survival, and the cycle of abuse (the abused becoming the abusers). 

This game has spawned a series that I personally believe to be one of the finest in the horror genre. This game, its sequel and prequel, the comics, and the audio series have crafted a world that is genuinely haunting but immensely interesting, I don't think I've ever been as immediately captivated by a game's world and lore than I have with Little Nightmares.

[h1]8.5/10[/h1]

Little Nightmares is dark, sinister, astounding, coarse and dark - all without the use of rated horror content or a first-person camera. It's a great horror puzzle adventure, which is amazingly atmospheric; where the scariest pieces are more of a fun gameplay experience than a playful horror. Little Nightmares is a well-designed, beautifully executed affair. It might be a bit longer, unless you go back a second, third, or fourth time just to collect all the collectibles. I guess the price reflects that, and if something's that good, maybe it's best to keep it on a pleasant length. There is a kind of repulsive, uncomfortable design everywhere. Doors are far too big for you, but also too big (or small) for some of the inhabitants of this world.  Rooms that should not physically exist are next to each other. It's all just familiar enough but twisted and impossible enough to create a feeling of discomfort and fear. And this is exactly where Little Nightmares succeeds.

I've always felt Little Nightmares shares a kindred spirit with INSIDE—perhaps the developers were inspired by PLAYDEAD's work to some extent. Little Nightmares' defining feature is its extensive use of set-piece storytelling, blending dystopian and mystical elements to craft an oppressive, eerie world and atmosphere. The most ingenious aspect is its masterful use of “emergent storytelling.” By deliberately leaving gaps in the narrative, it grants players ample room for imagination and interpretation.

However, the game remains somewhat weak overall and suffers from several noticeable flaws. First, the level design: while many objects in the environments are interactive, most interactions are essentially meaningless, purely wasting the player's time. While it offers some exploration freedom, it fails to integrate these interactions meaningfully with the plot or puzzles, which is a shame.

Second, the similar styles and color palettes across scenes result in a lack of truly striking, memorable environments. While most scenes leave some impression, none stand out as exceptional.

Thirdly, transitions between environments feel poorly executed. Moving from one area to another lacks a clear sense of spatial continuity or directional cues. While concept art hints at the game's setting—a vast, enclosed underwater world—this ambiguity inevitably blurs the player's perception of scene shifts.

Additionally, the game's controls feel somewhat clunky, with many button assignments being cumbersome and counterintuitive. For instance, grabbing, interacting, and grabbing edges after jumping are all handled by the same button. If you press the jump button while facing a high ledge but don't immediately press the grab button afterward, you won't latch onto the edge—a deeply counterintuitive experience. This becomes especially cumbersome when scenarios demand simultaneous high-intensity jumping, edge-grabbing, and item usage. Many first-time players I've observed spend a frustrating half-hour adapting to the controls, significantly detracting from the overall experience.

Furthermore, certain sections offer minimal margin for error, particularly when encountering enemies. This leads to frequent deaths for newcomers, severely disrupting the flow of gameplay. The game's most challenging achievement requires clearing the entire game without dying within one hour. I previously thought LIMBO's five-life run (unlimited time) was already grueling, but this takes it to a whole new level of frustration.

Finally, while the game incorporates many mystical and dystopian elements, I feel it lacks a certain depth. The overall atmosphere it builds is slightly underwhelming. The ending feels relatively conventional, lacking the profound impact delivered by the conclusions of INSIDE or LIMBO.

In summary, Little Nightmares is an exceptionally creative and stylistically unique work. However, my own stringent evaluation standards—coupled with an inevitable tendency to compare it to INSIDE—may have led me to notice certain imperfections. Nevertheless, this remains an outstanding game that I highly recommend. Incidentally, I believe the three DLCs add the perfect finishing touch, complementing the main game beautifully. DLC 3's ending, in particular, gave me goosebumps. I also strongly recommend experiencing the DLC content.

[h1][b]Overall, the game is decent, but due to its shortcomings, it left a negative impression on me.[/b][/h1]

[list]
[*]In terms of genre, Little Nightmares is a puzzle-platformer. However, one of the key aspects of this genre - controls - was not executed well enough. It's precisely because of the character's unresponsiveness that some sections become painfully difficult to complete. Often, the character gets stuck or jerks when interacting with the environment, and he is unresponsive and incredibly slow.

[*]In this game, deaths are probably one of the most unfair. In platforming sections or critical moments, the controls can be unreliable, and your character might not perform the necessary actions. Enemies aren't inherently dangerous, and they could be relatively easy to avoid, but sometimes it's really difficult to understand when they might notice you. Moreover, escaping from monsters is practically impossible, except when a hiding spot is immediately available, which isn't always the case. In such a case, it would be appropriate to have at least some way to escape, so that it wouldn't be a 100% death and level restart. For me, this just makes the stealth mechanics very annoying. Basically, it's not such a big problem, but it just adds extra inconvenience to an already too short game that's supposed to leave a positive impression.

[*]The environments, no matter how beautiful they are, are difficult to navigate. Due to the odd 2D/3D perspective, it's challenging to orient yourself in relation to your character's plane. When jumping onto a platform, you might find yourself slightly to the left or right of it. Interactive objects blend seamlessly with the environment and are easy to miss. There are many situations where you think you can climb somewhere, but it's actually impossible. This is especially frustrating in chase scenes, where you need to make quick decisions.

[*]At times, the static camera takes very inconvenient positions, making it impossible to understand your character's location. If something obstructs your view, you can't see your character, which is annoying. Strangely, the camera isn't tied to enemies, so there are instances where they can see you, but you can't. While you can move the camera using arrow keys (up-down-left-right), it's more of a crutch. Doing this consistently is difficult, primarily because of the control issues.

[*]Due to the size of the locations, you often have to run from one end to the other for a significant amount of time (and frustratingly, most puzzles involve finding keys or similar items on the opposite end of the map). Here, the problem also lies in the fact that solving such puzzles can be quite lingering, as they are not always intuitively clear.
[/list]

I believe these are the main reasons I personally didn't enjoy the game. I'm sure it has found its audience, and labeling it unplayable would be inaccurate. However, I found it difficult to get positive emotions by playing it, and this review is based on my personal experience.

[h3][i][b]P.S.[/b] In my review I considered the full game with 3 DLCs. So, if you disagree with certain points, it's possible that it might be related to the fact that you haven't experienced the additional game content.[/i][/h3]
